data.title: G-III Apparel Earnings Call Highlights Brand-Led Transition
data.description:
G-Iii Apparel ((GIII)) has held its Q2 earnings call. Read on for the main highlights of the call.

G-III Apparel’s latest earnings call struck a cautiously optimistic tone. Management highlighted a solid earnings beat, sharp margin expansion and a fortified balance sheet, even as reported sales declined and legacy Calvin Klein and Tommy Hilfiger revenue continued to roll off. Investors heard confidence in the go-forward brand portfolio and in the Marc Jacobs deal, despite near-term dilution and European weakness.

Second-Quarter Earnings Beat Guidance

Non-GAAP earnings per diluted share came in at $0.26, topping guidance of $0.15 to $0.25 and signaling stronger profitability than expected. Executives credited disciplined execution, tighter expense control and favorable mix as key factors, underscoring the company’s ability to deliver earnings growth even in a challenging demand backdrop.

Gross Margin Expanded Sharply

Gross margin jumped to 45.2% from 40.8% a year ago, a roughly 440 basis-point improvement that investors will view as a major highlight. The gains came from targeted price increases, healthier full-price selling and a deliberate push toward higher-margin owned brands, supported by ongoing cost-savings initiatives across sourcing and operations.

Go-Forward Portfolio Shows Resilience

Excluding Tommy Hilfiger and Calvin Klein, the go-forward brand portfolio posted high single-digit growth in the quarter. Wholesale sales in full-price channels for these brands climbed more than 20%, suggesting that the company’s future-facing platform is gaining traction even as legacy licensed revenue fades.

Marc Jacobs Acquisition Marks Strategic Pivot

Management framed the Marc Jacobs acquisition as transformational, positioning G-III as a brand-led global apparel powerhouse. The company now owns 100% of the Marc Jacobs operating business and holds a 50% earnings stake in the brand’s licensing via a joint venture with WHP Global, deepening its exposure to premium fashion.

Marc Jacobs Growth Avenues

Marc Jacobs currently derives roughly 90% of sales from handbags, small leather goods and accessories, leaving ample room to expand into new categories. G-III plans to grow ready-to-wear, fragrance, beauty, eyewear, children’s apparel, licensing and international wholesale, leveraging a network of more than 100 owned stores and strong direct-to-consumer economics.

Long-Term Marc Jacobs Revenue Potential

The Marc Jacobs operating business is expected to deliver about $360 million in global sales this year, excluding licensing income. Over the long term, management believes Marc Jacobs can scale to $1 billion in annual revenue for G-III, making it a central pillar of the company’s brand portfolio strategy.

Balance Sheet Strength and Liquidity

G-III ended the quarter with roughly $529 million in cash, up sharply from $302 million last year, and about $1 billion in available liquidity. Cash was boosted by around $134 million in tariff refunds including interest, and management emphasized that the balance sheet remains healthy even after the Marc Jacobs purchase, giving room to invest in growth.

Inventory Discipline and Capital Returns

Inventory fell about 13% versus a year ago, reflecting tighter inventory management and reduced risk of markdowns. The company also returned more than $12 million to shareholders through buybacks and dividends in the quarter, signaling confidence in its financial position while maintaining flexibility for strategic spending.

Donna Karan Performance Stands Out

Donna Karan delivered more than 45% sales growth in the quarter, fueled by strong consumer demand and aspirational positioning at full price. Digital traffic, conversion and average unit retail all improved, handbags posted double-digit gains and the dress business emerged as a key driver within the brand.

DKNY Maintains Solid Momentum

DKNY.com revenue rose in the mid-20% range year over year, supported by higher conversion and healthy average unit retail growth. Brick-and-mortar DKNY stores saw mid-single-digit comparable sales gains, while retail partners increased space allocations for Fall 2026 and Spring 2027, signaling confidence in the brand’s trajectory.

Karl Lagerfeld Extends Lifestyle Reach

Karl Lagerfeld posted strong growth in North America led by wholesale, and margins improved in Europe thanks to pricing and channel mix. The Karl Lagerfeld Jeans line continued to outperform internationally, while the brand pushed deeper into lifestyle with the first Karl Lagerfeld Café in Amsterdam and new residences and hotel projects.

Vilebrequin Delivers High Margins

Vilebrequin recorded positive growth across Europe, the Caribbean and Asia, with brand margins exceeding internal targets. Higher average unit retails and solid demand underpinned performance, complemented by a second limited-edition Fiat Topolino collaboration and the opening of the Vilebrequin La Plage Miami beach club.

Licensed Sports and Contemporary Brands Gain

The sports and lifestyle platform delivered healthy growth, helped by Starter’s limited-edition Pokémon jacket at Target and expanding Converse distribution. Levi’s was singled out as a quarterly highlight, while the contemporary portfolio, including French Connection and BCBG, continued to build momentum.

Strategic Investments and Cost Efficiencies

Management is investing in people, technology, marketing, Marc Jacobs product development, digital capabilities and retail experience to fuel future growth. At the same time, G-III plans to pursue previously announced cost-saving initiatives and identify new efficiencies, aiming to balance investment spending with margin preservation.

Sales Declines and PVH License Impact

Quarterly net sales fell about 10% to roughly $554 million and came in slightly below plan, largely due to planned reductions in Calvin Klein and Tommy Hilfiger revenue. Since PVH announced it would reclaim those licenses, G-III expects to have lost nearly $1.2 billion in revenue by year-end, with guidance embedding substantial ongoing declines.

European Market Challenges

Management described Europe as a difficult environment, citing macro softness, sharply lower traffic and heightened promotional activity. Struggling department stores in England, weaker travel from the Middle East and unusually warm weather weighed on sales, adding regional pressure on top of the PVH license wind-down.

Third-Quarter Headwinds and Earnings Decline

For the third quarter of fiscal 2027, G-III expects net sales of about $870 million versus $989 million a year ago, reflecting the biggest year-over-year reduction in PVH-related revenue. Non-GAAP net income is forecast at $59 million to $64 million, or $1.35 to $1.45 per share, down from $1.90 per share last year as the transition away from PVH weighs on earnings.

Initial Dilution from Marc Jacobs

Management acknowledged that Marc Jacobs will be dilutive for the first 12 months and slightly dilutive for the rest of fiscal 2027. However, the deal is expected to turn accretive thereafter, and leadership positioned the near-term drag as an acceptable cost to secure a high-potential, brand-centric growth engine.

Retail Margin and SG&A Pressure

Retail gross margin slipped to 50.6% from 52.4% last year, hurt by higher promotional activity during the quarter. SG&A expenses rose to $231 million from $227 million, excluding acquisition costs, as the company continued investing in talent, technology and marketing, causing some expense deleverage despite warehouse efficiency gains.

Tariffs and Delivery Timing Issues

Management flagged that tariffs impacted the business in a significant way last year and remain a headwind, with guidance assuming current rates persist. Weather-related delivery delays and missed containers also affected the timing of second-quarter sales, though the company expects most of that business to shift into subsequent periods.

Forward-Looking Guidance and Outlook

G-III reiterated fiscal 2027 net sales guidance of about $2.71 billion, down roughly 8% year over year, while raising non-GAAP EPS to $2.20 to $2.30 and adjusted EBITDA to $174 million to $178 million. The company anticipates close to 400 basis points of full-year gross margin improvement, net interest income of about $5 million, capex near $40 million and no further share repurchases, as Marc Jacobs scales toward a long-term $1 billion opportunity.

G-III’s earnings call painted a picture of a company in transition, trading near-term revenue and margin noise for a stronger brand-led future. With Donna Karan, DKNY, Karl Lagerfeld and Vilebrequin gaining traction, and Marc Jacobs positioned as a potential $1 billion-plus anchor, investors will be watching execution closely as PVH license losses roll off and margin gains become the key driver of shareholder value.
